title: Lattice Paths and Binary Strings
short: A path of right and up steps is a string of R's and U's, so a grid m steps wide and n steps tall has C(m + n, n) shortest paths.
trouble: Students count grid squares instead of steps, or count the paths through a point by adding the two parts instead of multiplying them.

blocks.html: A good way to count a hard set is to match its objects one-to-one with strings, and strings are easy to count. Grid paths are the classic example, and they explain the identities of Pascal's triangle.

A shortest path from $(0, 0)$ to $(m, n)$ along grid lines, moving right (R) or up (U), is the same thing as a string of $m$ R's and $n$ U's. So there are $\binom{m+n}{n}$ such paths. Paths through a point: multiply the paths to it by the paths from it.

Every shortest path uses exactly $m$ right steps and $n$ up steps, in some order, and every such order traces a different path. This is a bijection between paths and strings, so the counts are equal. A string of length $m + n$ is decided by choosing which $n$ of the positions are U's: $\binom{m+n}{n}$. Through a point $P$, a path is a first half (to $P$) followed by a second half (from $P$), and any first half fits any second half: that is the product rule.

blocks.title: Counting paths
blocks.q: How many shortest paths go from the bottom-left to the top-right corner of a grid $4$ blocks wide and $3$ blocks tall?
steps: Each path is a string of $4$ R's and $3$ U's: $7$ steps.

blocks.title: Through a point
blocks.q: In the same grid, how many shortest paths pass through $(2, 1)$?

blocks.title: Avoiding a point
blocks.q: In the same grid, how many shortest paths avoid $(2, 1)$?
steps: All paths minus the paths through it: $35 - 18 = 17$.
Check with the grid counts: set the count at $(2, 1)$ to $0$ and add up again from the corner; the far corner gets $17$.

blocks.html: Counting squares, or adding the two halves. A grid $4$ blocks wide has $5$ vertical lines, but a path takes only $4$ steps to the right; counting the squares or the lines instead of the steps gives the wrong string length. And paths through a point are (paths to it) times (paths from it), not plus. Check: the string must have exactly as many R's as the width and as many U's as the height.
